**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken by someone who wasn’t my mother, it was in a voice so thick with disdain that the syllables themselves seemed to curl like smoke. I was twelve, standing in the hallway of my new school, my backpack slung over one shoulder, my fingers twitching at my sides. The boy who said it—tall, with a smirk that didn’t reach his eyes—had called me *Ghulam*, as if the word were a brand, as if it explained everything about me that he didn’t want to know.

I didn’t correct him.

That was the first lesson: some names are gifts, some are curses, and some are just tools. Mine had been a tool for years before that, a quiet weapon in the hands of men who thought they owned me. My father had given it to me in a language that wasn’t his own, a language that tasted like iron and honey, a language that had been stolen and reshaped and passed down like a secret. He’d whispered it into my ear when I was small, his breath warm against my skin, his fingers tracing the shape of the letters in the air. *"This is who you are,"* he’d said. *"This is what they will call you."*

I didn’t know then that names could be unlearned.

---

The library was my sanctuary. The scent of old paper and polished wood, the way the light slanted through the stained-glass windows like liquid gold—it was a world where I could be anyone. I spent hours there, my nose buried in books, my fingers tracing the spines like braille. I read about kings and rebels, about women who burned cities and men who built them, about gods who loved and gods who lied. I read until my eyes stung, until the words blurred, until I forgot, for a few stolen hours, that I was just another girl with a name that didn’t fit.

But names are sticky things. They cling to you like dust, like the scent of curry and cigarette smoke that clung to my father’s clothes when he came home from the factory. They follow you into dreams. I dreamed of my name then—a voice, always a voice, calling me from the dark, pulling me toward something sharp and unseen. I’d wake gasping, my sheets damp with sweat, my heart hammering like a trapped bird.

One night, I woke to the sound of my own voice.

It wasn’t in my dreams. It was in the mirror.

I stood frozen, my reflection staring back at me with wide, unrecognizable eyes. The words had formed on my lips before I could stop them: *"I am not yours."*

The mirror didn’t answer. But something in the room did—a draft, maybe, or the creak of the old house settling. I turned, half-expecting to see a figure in the shadows, but there was nothing. Just the flicker of the candle on the nightstand, just the weight of the name still hanging between us, a ghost I couldn’t shake.

---

The first time I changed it, it was in a fit of rage.

I was sixteen, and my stepmother had called me *beti*—daughter—as if the word were a promise, as if it could erase the years of silence between us. I snapped. I spat the word back at her, then turned to the mirror and said, *"My name is not yours."*

I didn’t know what else to call myself. So I took the first name that came to mind, the name of a river in a story I’d read, the name of something wild and untamed. *Sindhu.*

It felt like a lie at first. Like a mask I’d slipped on too quickly, like a dress that was too big, too loose. But the more I said it, the more it stuck. The more I *became* it.

---

Names are power. They are the first thing people reach for when they want to own you. They are the last thing you have when you want to be free.

I learned this the hard way.

The first time I was arrested, the officer at the station looked at my ID and laughed. *"Sindhu?"* he said, as if the name were a joke. *"You think we don’t know who you really are?"* He reached for my wrist, his fingers bruising, and I saw the way his eyes flicked to the scar on my ankle—the one I’d gotten when I was twelve, when my father’s friend had thought it would teach me a lesson.

I didn’t fight him. I let him take me.

In the cell, the other women whispered. *"Ghulam,"* one of them said, as if the word alone could break me. But I didn’t flinch. I sat on the concrete floor, my back straight, my hands folded in my lap, and I waited.

Names are just words, after all. And words can be unlearned.

---

Now, when people ask me my name, I give them *Sindhu*. Sometimes, if they press, I tell them the truth. But most of the time, I let them wonder.

It’s a game, really. A game of power, of memory, of the things we carry with us like ghosts.

I don’t know if I’ll ever be free of it. But I know this: the name that was given to me was never mine to keep.

And that’s enough.
